**Course source:** Day 1 §6–7. **Running system:** Order, Product, and User services.

## Why the course introduces Ribbon

In the historical Spring Cloud stack, Ribbon supplies a client-side load-balancing layer. Order asks for a Product endpoint by service name, and the client chooses one of the discovered instances.

Conceptually:

~~~text
Order invokes "product" -> Ribbon rule -> Product A or Product B
                                     -> send HTTP request
~~~

The course builds several Product instances and changes the invocation path so Order no longer needs to encode one provider address.

## Selection rules and limitations

**Round robin** alternates eligible instances. **Random** selection uses no predictable sequence. Other policies may incorporate response times or availability history. These are choices about **which endpoint**, not a solution to business idempotency.

When a chosen instance fails, a client may retry elsewhere according to configuration, but retries can increase load and must respect request deadlines. Retrying order creation with no idempotency key can produce duplicates.

## Original simplified example

Our Node lab implements one round-robin expression. Calling the order endpoint repeatedly reveals that orders may be served by different Product instances; inspect the Product service response directly or add logging if studying routing decisions.

~~~js
const index = nextProduct++ % productInstances.length;
const url = productInstances[index];
~~~

This is **not Ribbon code**; it demonstrates the same architectural decision without copying the course sample.

## Modernisation

Ribbon belongs to an older Spring Cloud integration generation. For current Spring Cloud projects, review **Spring Cloud LoadBalancer** and the current release train rather than importing Ribbon from the course's dependency list.

Useful reference: [Spring Cloud LoadBalancer](https://docs.spring.io/spring-cloud-commons/reference/spring-cloud-commons/loadbalancer.html).
